summary: In this Holy Week and Pascha special episode, Fr. Andrew Stephen Damick and Fr. Stephen De Young explore the biblical and ancient Near Eastern background of Christ's descent into Hades (the Harrowing of Hell). They begin by examining the Baal Cycle from Ugaritic texts, showing how Psalm 24 (23 LXX) directly polemicizes against Baal mythology, asserting that Yahweh, not Baal, is the true conqueror of chaos and death. The psalm's imagery of 'lifting up the gates' is shown to be a taunt against Baal's failed rebellion, and is fulfilled in Christ's victorious entry into Hades. The second half focuses on the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15), interpreting the crossing of the Reed Sea as a passage through death to life, with Yahweh defeating the Egyptian gods, especially the war god Montu. The third half examines Hosea 13:14 and 1 Corinthians 15:55, revealing that 'Death' (Mavet/Thanatos) and 'Sheol/Hades' are personified as Canaanite deities, along with their servants Deber (Pestilence) and Keteb (Plague). The hosts demonstrate how these demonic powers are disarmed by Christ's death and resurrection, and how Orthodox liturgical practices—such as the Paschal vigil and funeral services—preserve this ancient understanding. The episode concludes with a reading from the Gospel of Nicodemus, depicting the dramatic confrontation between Christ and the powers of hell.

entities.title: Baal
entities.summary: Canaanite storm god, son of El, whose mythology is recounted in the Baal Cycle from Ugarit. He is depicted as a rebellious deity who attempts to overthrow Yam and Nahar but ends up in the underworld. In the Bible, Baal worship is condemned, and Yahweh is shown as the true Lord.

entities.title: Yam and Nahar
entities.summary: Canaanite gods of the sea (Yam) and river (Nahar), representing chaos. In the Baal Cycle, Baal rebels against them. In Psalm 24, Yahweh is said to have founded the earth upon them, asserting his dominion over chaos.

entities.title: Mot
entities.summary: Canaanite god of death, also known as Mavet. He is the ruler of the underworld and is depicted as a devouring mouth. In Hosea 13:14, Yahweh taunts Mot, declaring that he will redeem his people from his hand.

entities.title: Deber and Keteb
entities.summary: Canaanite deities of pestilence and plague, servants of Mot. They are mentioned in Hosea 13:14, Habakkuk 3, and Psalm 91. In Orthodox tradition, they are recognized as demons, and Psalm 91 is used as an exorcism and in funeral services.

entities.title: Montu
entities.summary: Egyptian war god, depicted as the right arm of Ra. In Exodus 15, Yahweh's 'right hand' and 'strong arm' are polemical references to Montu, asserting that Yahweh, not Montu, is the true warrior who defeats Pharaoh.

entities.title: Ugarit
entities.summary: Ancient city in northwestern Syria, destroyed circa 1180 BC. Its discovery in the 20th century yielded clay tablets with the Baal Cycle and other texts, providing crucial context for understanding biblical polemics against Canaanite religion.

entities.title: Sheol
entities.summary: The Hebrew term for the underworld, often personified as a deity or a gaping mouth. In the Old Testament, it is the abode of the dead, from which Yahweh rescues the righteous.

concepts.title: Harrowing of Hell
concepts.summary: The doctrine that after his death, Christ descended into Hades/Sheol to rescue the righteous dead, breaking the power of death and the devil. This is a central theme of Holy Saturday and Pascha.

concepts.title: Divine Smack Talk
concepts.summary: The biblical practice of using polemical language against pagan gods, asserting that attributes and deeds claimed for them actually belong to Yahweh. Examples include Psalm 24 against Baal and Exodus 15 against Egyptian gods.

concepts.title: Sacred Geography
concepts.summary: The concept that physical locations have spiritual significance and can represent or become gateways to spiritual realities, such as the Reed Sea representing the boundary between life and death.

concepts.title: Passing Through Death to Life
concepts.summary: The theme that God does not spare his people from death but leads them through it to resurrection, as seen in the Exodus crossing of the Reed Sea and in Christian baptism.

concepts.title: Disarmament of Death
concepts.summary: The idea that through his death and resurrection, Christ stripped the powers of death and the devil of their weapons (sin, law, plague, pestilence), rendering them powerless.

claims.text: Psalm 24 is a direct polemic against the Baal Cycle, asserting that Yahweh, not Baal, is the conqueror of chaos and the rightful king who enters the underworld to rescue the dead.

The Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) depicts Yahweh's victory over the Egyptian gods, especially Montu, and portrays the crossing of the Reed Sea as a passage through death to life, not merely a military escape.
Hosea 13:14 personifies Death (Mot) and Sheol as deities, and mentions their servants Deber and Keteb. Yahweh taunts them, declaring that he will redeem his people from their grasp.

The Orthodox Church's liturgical use of Psalm 24 (23) at the Paschal vigil and in funeral services preserves the original ancient context of Christ's harrowing of hell, even though the Baal Cycle was lost for millennia.
Through his death and resurrection, Christ disarmed the powers of death and the devil, stripping them of their weapons (sin, law, plague, pestilence) and rendering them powerless.

scriptural_links.summary: Interpreted as a polemic against the Baal Cycle, with verses 7-10 describing Christ's entry into Hades. Used in Orthodox Paschal vigil and funeral services.
The Song of the Sea, depicting Yahweh's victory over Egyptian gods and the crossing of the Reed Sea as a passage through death to life. Used in baptismal liturgy.
Yahweh taunts Death (Mot) and Sheol, asking where their plagues (Deber and Keteb) are. Quoted by St. Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:55.
Quotes Hosea 13:14, taunting death and the grave. Used in the Paschal sermon of St. John Chrysostom.
Mentions Deber (pestilence) and Keteb (plague) as demons. Used as an exorcism psalm and in funeral services.
States that Christ destroyed the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil.

glossary.definition: A collection of Ugaritic tablets recounting the mythology of the god Baal, including his rebellion against Yam and Nahar, his victory, and his descent into the underworld.
Hebrew for 'Reed Sea' or 'Sea of the End,' the body of water crossed by the Israelites in the Exodus. It also refers to the Egyptian mythological boundary between life and death.
The Christian doctrine that Christ descended into Hades after his death to rescue the righteous dead, breaking the power of death and the devil.
The Orthodox service on Holy Saturday night/Easter morning, which includes a procession, the chanting of Psalm 24, and the proclamation of Christ's resurrection.
An apocryphal text (4th century) containing a detailed account of Christ's descent into Hades, including dialogues between Satan, Hell, and the saints.
